title: Question about Ivan the Terrible by Sergei Eisenstein

commenti.body:
I didn't consider this to be intentionally funny in the specific way you described. I think those close-ups were considered to be pretty key to Eisenstein's work, and he would use them for dramatic effect- similar to how Wells would use those types of close-ups in Citizen Kane. 

As a piece, I found it more akin to the sincerity of John Ford or Frank Capra movies. The use of melodrama, humor, and mythos that ties into national propaganda is all there for the taking. But I found the humor light and sparse compared to the very real emotional ask that this movie is making. 

I think sincerity is often lacking in modern day cinema because it was washed out by so many different film movements, so to find true sentimental film can often feel odd, especially watching it now and looking back. Take this scene from [Ivan the Terrible](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iKpcBSRvco0&ab_channel=TheaestheticoftheImage%3A%5Bworld%5Dcinemaclips) and compare it to [Mr. Smith Goes to Washington](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7Yd3ouQsPFY&ab_channel=pataylor1965) and it conveys the same type of emotional resonance (and propaganda) that the director is going for. 

Most of Eisenstein's films, and many Soviet films from this time period have this look and feel. First, I think acting was noticeably different during this period, and even more so because it's Soviet. Melodramatic acting was huge- even in Hollywood, and Eisenstein and many others were coming out of an era where most of their films relied only on image, so lots of the emotionality is conveyed on screen rather than in dialogue. On a similar note, many Soviet theaters often lacked the proper equipment to project sound, rendering dialogue-heavy films less desirable.  

This is also the age of propaganda. Eisenstein's films are set to convey the Soviet education program that these films were intended to show what good citizens needed to know. In this film, you can see how Eisenstein is showing the cause of unification and the need for a powerful dictator, even if they may be ruthless in their actions \*cough- Stalin- cough\*. 

If you don't like this rigid melodrama and sentimentality- I totally get it, it's definitely not for everyone and takes a mindset to sit through it all. But I don't think this was made to be laughed at.

I don't think it should be understood as propaganda as such, Eisenstein really had that feeling for the historical situation.

Regarding humor, many scenes in their films have a light-hearted portrayal, but they still take themselves very seriously, for example those scenes in Strike where they show the poor, we can see them as funny, but it is more of a way of narrating. of the time.

Today we can see it as endearing because our cinema has evolved and taken that language in a different way.

It is absolutely agitprop. The themes of Eisenstein changed with the dictates of the Soviet Union. The collectivist heroes of October and The Old and the New gave way to the great unifiers of Nevsky and Ivan. These restraints were directly or indirectly passed down from authorities.

Eisenstein not only had the intention of making propaganda, he was part of that context and it is very understandable that he was committed to it, I don't know that much about history, but I imagine what such a big social change must have been for someone who was experiencing it.

He himself wrote about cinema's ability to foster social change, but there is an artistic intention in representing his reality.

Thanks for the thorough and detailed response and for providing some context. It wasn’t so much that I didn’t like the film, but maybe just that I found it hard to appreciate in the same way as audiences who were viewing and responding to it at the time of its release.  Also, that’s interesting about the theaters not having sound projecting equipment and how that ended up affecting the films being produced. I thought the theatricality, limited dialogue and over exaggerated acting might have also had something to do with the lingering influence of the silent film era.

The film was directly commissioned by Stalin during WW2. The golden mongol horse on one side and Teutonic knights on the other are clear representations of fighting the Japanese and Germans. The Teutonic knights helmets are even reimagined to look more like Nazi WW2 helmets.

I find it hilarious too, and one of the best movies ever made. It plays magnificently in a theater if you can catch the full two parts, with the color reel. It's absolutely on purpose; Eisenstein isn't an idiot, the satire is part and parcel. Ditto the grotesquerie. A telltale sign of satire is extremity of effect. He's pretending to celebrate a historic figure but he's really talking about the present, and about myth-making and propaganda. About political power, which is itself an exaggerated representation of the will of the people the politicians ostensibly represent. It's a giant exaggerated face so that you know 100% it's an exaggerated portrayal, larger than life. It's by design. Eisentstein left behind thousands of detailed drawings which confirm this (should you really doubt it, ha) - the face in profile, and his body in long shot with his ever-more-hunched shoulders, is presented as more and more explicitly vulture-ish as time passes within the film and he gets more and more corrupted by the things he has to do to maintain his precarious position, surrounded on all sides by enemies. 

IMO the act of making the film was really one of unprecedented courage; it is an absolutely scathing indictment of Russian history that is totally misrepresenting itself as bootlicking feel-good propaganda. Famously, Part 1 fooled Stalin, but Part 2 didn't. There is no Part 3.

The score too reflects the satiric intent, Prokofiev is totally in tune with Eisenstein. They worked in harmony, collaborating on every frame. The greatest score ever composed <3 

You'll find the humorous quality absent from Alexander Nevsky, a film which really is propaganda. There's no satire at all there and though the score is no less good it is totally a straightforward heroic glorification thing and a lot less interesting.
